title: Working at Redwood — careers, hiring, onboarding, benefits, and internal tools
author: Avery Chen
summary: Comprehensive reference for new and existing Redwood employees covering how we work, role expectations and promotion criteria, hiring and onboarding workflows, benefits & perks, and the core internal tools and access controls.
body:
Overview

This page consolidates core People Ops guidance for working at Redwood. It is intended for new hires, managers, and any employee who needs a single authoritative source for role expectations, hiring and onboarding workflows, benefits, and the primary internal tools and access controls.

1) Working at Redwood — culture & expectations

Intro: Redwood values engineering excellence, product-driven iteration, and operational responsibility. We prioritize shipping reliable inference products while maintaining a supportive culture of learning and ownership.

Key behaviors we expect from all employees:
- Own outcomes: adopt SLO-oriented thinking for product and operational work.
- Be customer-minded: understand how your work impacts developer UX and cost/perf tradeoffs.
- Collaborate inclusively: asynchronous-first communication, clear RFCs, and cross-team code reviews.
- Learn continuously: use postmortems, retros, and regular feedback to improve.

Working hours and flexibility:
- Core overlap expectations: teams typically expect 2–4 hours of overlap with core US-Pacific working hours.
- Flexible remote-first policy: heads of team to publish team-specific on-site cadence.
- Time off: see Benefits & Perks section for PTO policy.

2) Roles, career ladders & leveling

Scope: This section summarizes engineering and product individual contributor (IC) levels and promotion expectations. For full manager ladder and leadership tracks, see the People Ops ladder pages linked at the bottom.

Engineering IC ladder (common shorthand):
- E3 (Associate Engineer): delivers tasks with mentorship; focuses on project-level scope.
- E4 (Software Engineer): independently delivers medium-sized features and owns code quality.
- E5 (Senior Engineer): drives design across projects, mentors others, owns cross-service concerns.
- E6 (Principal Engineer): influences architecture, leads multi-team initiatives, and sets technical direction.
- E7 (Distinguished/Staff): company-wide technical leadership, long-term strategy, external representation where relevant.

Promotion criteria (summary):
- Impact: measurable improvements in product metrics, latency, cost, or developer velocity.
- Scope & Autonomy: increases in the scale of problems owned and independence.
- Craft: code quality, design clarity, and technical judgment.
- Leadership & Mentorship: growing evidence of mentoring, recruiting, and cross-team influence.

Process for promotion:
1. Candidate prepares a promotion packet: summary of impact, 3–5 cross-functional references, timeline, and exemplar work.
2. Manager reviews and submits packet to People Ops.
3. Promotion calibration committee meets monthly; outcome communicated within two weeks of the meeting.

3) Hiring process overview (for hiring managers & interviewers)

Goals: hire diverse, high-impact engineers and product folks who align with Redwood values. The process below is prescriptive to maintain consistency and candidate experience.

Stages (standard for engineering roles):
1. Requisition & intake: hiring manager files req in Greenhouse with role profile and compensation band; People Ops approves.
2. Sourcing & screening: Recruiter screens and schedules a 30–45m phone screen.
3. Interview loop: 4–6 interviews including coding/design, system design, culture fit, and a collaboration exercise. Interviewers must use the rubric and submit written notes within 24 hours.
4. Debrief & decision: panel meets within 48 hours to reach consensus. Offer approvals require hiring manager, recruiter, and People Ops sign-off.
5. Offer & negotiation: standard offer template used; comp band visible to hiring manager.
6. Background & compliance checks: initiated upon offer acceptance.

Interviewer responsibilities:
- Read the candidate brief before the interview.
- Use the standardized rubric (technical, communication, system thinking, ownership).
- Provide timely, objective feedback with examples.

4) Onboarding — first 90 days (manager + new hire checklist)

Principles: make onboarding predictable, reduce cognitive overhead, and enable early impact.

Manager checklist (pre-boarding and first 30 days):
- Pre-boarding: ensure Okta account, laptop and accessories provisioned, GitHub access requested, Slack invite sent, and initial calendar holds for 1:1s.
- Day 1: team welcome, security briefing, and first contribution task assigned (small bug or docs change).
- Week 1: schedule walkthroughs for core stack (serving runtime, infra, console), pair on first task, and review goals.
- Month 1: 30-day check-in to review ramp, blockers, and learning plan.
- Month 3: formal 90-day review meeting with documented outcomes and updated goals.

New hire checklist (first 90 days):
1. Complete mandatory trainings: security basics, data handling, and privacy.
2. Complete paperwork: payroll, equity, and benefits enrollment (timelines noted in People Ops portal).
3. Ship first non-trivial contribution: submit a PR with tests and receive a peer review.
4. Schedule career conversation with manager to align on expectation and learning plan.

Onboarding resources:
- People Ops portal (policy and benefits enrollment)
- Engineering quickstarts repo (internal GitHub)
- Team-specific runbooks and system diagrams in Confluence

5) Benefits & perks (high level)

Health & wellness:
- Medical, dental, vision plans with employer contribution levels; new hires enrolled within 30 days.
- Mental health support: EAP and paid counseling sessions.

Time off & leave:
- PTO: flexible unlimited policy with guideline of 15–25 days average usage encouraged; team-specific blackout windows communicated by managers.
- Parental leave: 16 weeks primary caregiver, 8 weeks secondary caregiver (paid).
- Paid holidays: company-designated holidays plus floating holidays.

Financial & retirement:
- 401(k) with company match up to 4% after 3 months of service.
- Equity grants per role level, documented in offer.

Learning & growth perks:
- Learning stipend: $1,500/year for courses, conferences, and books.
- Mentor program and internal tech talks.

Office & equipment:
- Remote-first equipment allowance: $1,200 one-time for home office setup plus choice of laptop (MacBook Pro or Linux laptop) and external monitors.
- Commuter stipend for employees using office locations.

Perks & culture:
- Quarterly team budgets for offsites and social activities.
- Regular hack weeks and innovation days.

Benefits enrollment timelines and detailed plan summaries live on the People Ops benefits page (link at bottom).

6) Internal tools — access, guides, and common workflows

Core tools & short guidance:
- Okta (SSO): primary identity provider. Managers request application access via the People Ops portal.
- Slack: primary communication. Important channels: #announcements, #sre-alerts, #dev-general, #product-roadmap. Use threads and reactions to keep channels tidy.
- GitHub (org: redwood-inference): repo ownership is enforced via CODEOWNERS; open PRs should have at least two reviewers for feature changes and one reviewer for docs.
- Confluence: source of truth for runbooks, design docs, and team pages. Use templates for RFCs and runbooks.
- Jira: issue tracking; teams own their boards and set sprint cadences.
- Redwood Console (internal): production observability and tracing; access requires manager approval and SSO. Follow the Observability Standards page for dashboard ownership.
- CLI & deployments: redwoodctl is the canonical deployment CLI. Only on-call and release engineers have prod deploy permissions by default. Requests for temporary access handled via the change-management process.

Access & security practices:
- Principle of least privilege: request only the access necessary for your role.
- Privileged access reviews happen quarterly; owners will be notified for attestation.
- Secrets & keys: store secrets in the company vault (KMS/HSM-backed) and do not commit credentials to Git.

Sample quick-start commands (internal use):
- Clone the engineering quickstarts repo: git clone git@github.com:redwood-inference/engineering-quickstarts.git
- Run local dev with docker-compose: make dev (see repo README for pre-reqs)
- Install CLI: curl -sSL https://internal.redwood.com/install.sh | bash

7) Manager guide — hiring and development responsibilities

Hiring responsibilities:
- Keep job descriptions up to date and inclusive.
- Partner with recruiting to maintain a healthy pipeline.
- Ensure interviewers read the candidate brief and use the rubric.

People development responsibilities:
- Hold regular 1:1s and career conversations; document goals in the HRIS.
- Run quarterly calibration with peers for promotion readiness.
- Ensure performance feedback is timely and evidence-based.

8) Policies & escalation

Key policies (links): data handling, acceptable use, code of conduct, conflict of interest. When in doubt, contact security@redwood.com or people-ops@redwood.com.

Incidents and urgent issues:
- Production incident first responder: follow the on-call runbook in Confluence.
- Escalation path: on-call -> SRE lead -> CTO -> CEO (for Sev1 customer-impacting incidents).

9) FAQs & common scenarios

Q: How do I request hardware beyond the standard allowance?
A: Submit a request to people-ops@redwood.com with justification; managers approve purchases within team budgets.

Q: Who approves time off for company-wide events?
A: Managers approve PTO; for company-wide blackout periods the Exec team will notify in advance.
